title: $4 Billion to $36 Billion in Six Months: Swaps, "Marking the Close", and Counterparties Who Had Started Asking
participants: Prime brokers and security-based swap counterparties
Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The growth figure is the Commission's headline and it is the whole shape of the case: the scheme alleged "increased Archegos's assets under management from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in just under six months", achieved "largely through the entry into SBSs with about a dozen Counterparties".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What the instrument did was hold the exposure off anyone's view but the counterparty's. Security-based swaps gave Archegos "significant exposure to rising and falling share prices of the issuers referenced in its SBSs" without the firm appearing as the holder, and with about a dozen counterparties each seeing only their own slice of a book none of them saw whole.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is alleged to have been deliberate and specific. Archegos "knowingly provided these Counterparties with false assurances concerning its portfolio composition, its concentrated exposure, and its liquidity profile", which "fraudulently convinced its Counterparties that Archegos's overall positioning was less concentrated and more liquid than it actually was". The point of the deception was capacity: it "induced Archegos's Counterparties to continue to transact with it and extend leverage beyond what the Counterparties' risk tolerance would have otherwise permitted had they known the truth".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was a price the firm set for itself. The Commission alleges Archegos "chose not to rely on ordinary market forces" and instead manipulated the market in its top ten holdings "by dominating the market" for them, by "setting the tone" with large pre-market trading, "by bidding up prices by entering incrementally higher limit orders throughout the trading day", and by "marking the close" with large trading in the final thirty minutes — "all with the goal of artificially inflating the share prices of its Top 10 Holdings". The inflated marks then supported the margin that funded the next round.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment came two years later, and it fell on the bank rather than the fund. On 24 July 2023 the Federal Reserve announced a consent order and a $268.5 million fine with UBS for misconduct by Credit Suisse, finding "unsafe and unsound counterparty credit risk management practices" and stating that "During Credit Suisse’s relationship with Archegos, Credit Suisse failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings." FINMA, acting the same day, "found that Credit Suisse had seriously and systematically violated financial market law in the context of its business relationship with the Archegos family office", ordered corrective measures from UBS as legal successor, and opened proceedings against a former Credit Suisse manager. The Federal Reserve and Prudential Regulation Authority penalties totalled approximately $387 million — against a Credit Suisse loss the Board puts at approximately $5.5 billion.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Security-based swaps as a route to equity exposure that does not appear in the holder's own disclosure, and prime brokerage relationships in which each counterparty prices the risk of a client whose total book it cannot see.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Archegos tightening of security-based swap position reporting and of prime-broker counterparty risk practice, and a set of concluded enforcement actions — a Federal Reserve consent order, a FINMA finding, a Prudential Regulation Authority penalty — directed at the counterparties’ risk management rather than at the fund.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Margin extended by the counterparties funded the trading that inflated the prices; the inflated prices raised the value of the collateral; the richer collateral justified more margin. The loop ran until a price it did not set moved against it.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Archegos was a freak event — one secretive family office that fooled a dozen of the most sophisticated banks in the world, who were its victims.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The complaint does allege deception of the counterparties, and that half stands. But the banks-as-victims reading does not survive the regulators. The Federal Reserve’s July 2023 consent order found Credit Suisse’s counterparty credit risk management "unsafe and unsound" and stated that it "failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings" — "despite repeated warnings" being the Board’s phrase, not an inference drawn here. FINMA found that in the same relationship Credit Suisse had "seriously and systematically violated financial market law". The SEC’s own complaint says the deception worked "despite varying degrees and quality of risk management and proactive questioning of Archegos by its Counterparties", and that "certain of Archegos’s Counterparties already had begun asking Archegos questions to evaluate its risk profile" before the relevant period began. Nor was the fund merely secretive: it is alleged to have been setting the prices of its own collateral by pre-market trading, incremental limit orders and marking the close. What remains allegation is what the SEC alleges against the individuals; the findings against the bank are concluded regulatory actions. The dossier keeps the two apart.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: An SEC complaint filed in the Southern District of New York on 27 April 2022 alleging that between March 2020 and March 2021 Archegos grew from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in assets under management — the Commission’s press release putting it as "approximately $1.5 billion with $10 billion in exposure in March 2020 to a value of more than $36 billion with $160 billion in exposure at its peak" — largely through security-based swaps with about a dozen counterparties; that it manipulated the market in its top ten holdings by dominating trading, setting the tone pre-market, entering incrementally higher limit orders and marking the close; and that it gave counterparties false assurances about exposure, concentration and liquidity to obtain trading capacity. Those are allegations. What is concluded, by consent and by finding: the Federal Reserve’s $268.5 million fine on UBS for Credit Suisse’s "unsafe and unsound counterparty credit risk management practices", its statement that Credit Suisse "failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings", and approximately $5.5 billion of Credit Suisse losses from the default; FINMA’s finding that Credit Suisse "seriously and systematically violated financial market law" in the relationship, with corrective measures ordered against UBS and proceedings opened against a former manager; and combined Federal Reserve and Prudential Regulation Authority penalties of approximately $387 million.

citations.title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Sung Kook (Bill) Hwang, Patrick Halligan, William Tomita and Scott Becker, Complaint, No. 1:22-cv-03402 (S.D.N.Y., filed 27 April 2022)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. EVERYTHING BELOW IS AN ALLEGATION IN A CIVIL COMPLAINT, NOT A FINDING. The Summary alleges "a fraudulent scheme by Defendants that included interlocking deceptive acts and misconduct, through false and misleading statements to security-based swap ('SBS') counterparties and prime brokers (collectively, 'Counterparties') and manipulative trading designed to artificially move the market, which, in tandem, increased Archegos's assets under management from around $4 billion to over $36 billion in just under six months." On the instrument: "From March 2020 until its collapse in March 2021, Archegos, at Hwang's direction, underwent a period of rapid and exponential growth, achieved largely through the entry into SBSs with about a dozen Counterparties, which subjected Archegos to significant exposure to rising and falling share prices of the issuers referenced in its SBSs." On the alleged manipulation: Archegos "engaged in a brazen scheme to manipulate the market for the securities of the issuers that represented Archegos's top 10 holdings", "effected this scheme by dominating the market for its Top 10 Holdings, as well as by 'setting the tone' (i.e., engaging in large pre-market trading), bidding up prices by entering incrementally higher limit orders throughout the trading day, and 'marking the close' (i.e., engaging in large trading in the last 30 minutes of the trading day) and by other non-economic trading, all with the goal of artificially inflating the share prices of its Top 10 Holdings." On the fuel: "The margin and capacity extended by Archegos's Counterparties served as the fuel for its manipulative trading", and the defendants are alleged to have "deliberately misled many of Archegos's Counterparties" with "false assurances concerning its portfolio composition, its concentrated exposure, and its liquidity profile", which "induced Archegos's Counterparties to continue to transact with it and extend leverage beyond what the Counterparties' risk tolerance would have otherwise permitted had they known the truth". A DETAIL THAT CUTS AGAINST THE BANKS-AS-VICTIMS READING, in the complaint's own words: "as of the beginning of the Relevant Period, certain of Archegos's Counterparties already had begun asking Archegos questions to evaluate its risk profile", and the deception succeeded "despite varying degrees and quality of risk management and proactive questioning of Archegos by its Counterparties". On the collapse: over "less than a week in late March 2021, the house of cards collapsed", and the default "resulted in billions of dollars in credit losses among its Counterparties and significant losses to the market participants who invested in the stocks at inflated prices." The criminal proceedings that followed were NOT sourced for this dossier and no verdict or sentence is asserted in it.

citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, "SEC Charges Archegos and its Founder with Massive Market Manipulation Scheme", Press Release 2022-70, 27 April 2022
citations.quoteOrFact: Read in full from sec.gov. THIS CITATION WAS INHERITED WITH A PLACEHOLDER: its previous quoteOrFact read only "Source carried over from the Crash Conduits entry 'archegos-swap-implosion-2021'" — a URL migrated from a legacy page and never opened. It has now been opened and read, and the text below is what the page says. The Commission announced charges against Sung Kook (Bill) Hwang "with orchestrating a fraudulent scheme that resulted in billions of dollars in losses", together with chief financial officer Patrick Halligan, head trader William Tomita and chief risk officer Scott Becker. On the instrument: "The SEC's complaint alleges that, from at least March 2020 to March 2021, Hwang purchased on margin billions of dollars of total return swaps. These security-based swaps allow investors to take on huge positions in equity securities of companies by posting limited funds up front." On the alleged purpose: "Hwang frequently entered into certain of these swaps without any economic purpose other than to artificially and dramatically drive up the prices of the various companies' securities, which induced other investors to purchase those securities at inflated prices." THE SCALE FIGURES, which are fuller than the complaint's own summary: Archegos increased "in value from approximately $1.5 billion with $10 billion in exposure in March 2020 to a value of more than $36 billion with $160 billion in exposure at its peak in March 2021." The release also records the alleged deception of counterparties "about Archegos's exposure, concentration and liquidity, in order to get increased trading capacity". A press release describing allegations in a complaint; it establishes no fact against any defendant.

citations.title: Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA), "Archegos: FINMA concludes proceedings against Credit Suisse", press release, 24 July 2023
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from FINMA's own site. INHERITED WITH A PLACEHOLDER quoteOrFact ("Source carried over from the Crash Conduits entry") and now actually opened and read. This is a REGULATORY FINDING, not an allegation, and it is about the bank rather than the fund: "In the course of its enforcement proceedings, the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA found that Credit Suisse had seriously and systematically violated financial market law in the context of its business relationship with the Archegos family office. FINMA is ordering corrective measures from its legal successor, UBS. In addition, FINMA has opened enforcement proceedings against a former Credit Suisse manager." On scale: "In March 2021, several investment banks incurred large losses due to the collapse of the Archegos hedge fund. Credit Suisse suffered the biggest loss of over USD 5 billion." On the instrument, in FINMA's own description: "the Archegos family office took synthetic (i.e. without owning the corresponding stock) stock positions (“long” or “short” depending on price expectations) with investment banks such as Credit Suisse. These are instruments that replicate the performance of an underlying asset, for example, a share (total return swaps)." FINMA records that it "took various immediate risk-reducing measures in April 2021" and that "At the same time as FINMA, the authorities in the USA and the UK are also announcing their findings in this matter." Note on the source: the page is served from a multilingual site whose title element came back in French on fetch; the body read and quoted here is the English text.

citations.title: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, consent order and $268.5 million fine with UBS Group AG for misconduct by Credit Suisse, press release, 24 July 2023
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from the Board's own site. INHERITED WITH A PLACEHOLDER quoteOrFact and now opened and read. This is an enforcement action concluded by consent, and it is the most important document for the counterparty half of this dossier: "The Federal Reserve Board on Monday announced a consent order and a $268.5 million fine with UBS Group AG, of Zurich, Switzerland, for misconduct by Credit Suisse, which UBS subsequently acquired in June 2023. The misconduct involved Credit Suisse's unsafe and unsound counterparty credit risk management practices with its former counterparty, Archegos Capital Management LP. In 2021, Credit Suisse suffered approximately $5.5 billion in losses because of the default of Archegos, an investment fund. During Credit Suisse's relationship with Archegos, Credit Suisse failed to adequately manage the risk posed by Archegos despite repeated warnings." The Board required Credit Suisse "to improve counterparty credit risk management practices and to address additional longstanding deficiencies in other risk management programs at Credit Suisse's U.S. operations", and records that the action was taken "in conjunction with actions by the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority and the Bank of England's Prudential Regulation Authority", with the Board's and the PRA's penalties totalling "approximately $387 million". The phrase "despite repeated warnings" is the Board's.
